newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end a shade lower, financials weak.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end a shade lower, financials weak.

text.p: Tokyo stocks ended a shade lower on Friday after indices had wandered within a narrow range throughout the day, weighed down by weakness in the bank and securities sectors, brokers said. They said a wait-and-see mood was strong ahead of the fiscal year-end, muffling activity.
The Nikkei average finished down 20.70 points or 0.11 percent at 18,189.72. Its June futures were up 20 at 18,210.

"Participants, especially dealers, were reluctant to take up fresh positions ahead of the weekend and the new business year, although there was some window-dressing activity," said Seiki Orimi, an analyst at Dai-Ichi Securities.

Turnover was a scant 259 million shares, the first time it has fallen below 300 million since January 7. On Thursday, 493 million shares changed hands. Losers on Friday totalled 514 and gainers 494, while 211 issues were steady.

"In past years, year-end window-dressing activity inflated turnover to around 500 million shares," a "Big Four" broker said. "Participants feel the present state of the indices is sufficient to end the year on and are sitting back to wait."
Brokers said due to the thin trade, losses in the banking and securities sectors pressured the indices, the TOPIX index in particular.

It ended 3.87 points or 0.28 percent lower at 1,378.71. The Nikkei 300 shed 1.25 points or 0.47 percent to 265.19. The second section index fell 2.48 points or 0.15 percent to 1,645.70. Turnover was 11.70 million, up from 5.66 million the previous day. The over-the-counter index was down 5.32 points or 0.47 percent at 1,135.32 in late trade.

News that Japanese financial authorities are considering asking major Japanese banks to provide funds to aid debt-ridden Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB) was a relief for NCB, but was seen as an additional burden for the banks and drove shares in the sector lower, traders said.
NCB ended down two yen at 289 and was the most actively traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo bourse, with 12.134 million shares changing hands.

Sakura Bank Ltd lost 36 yen to 714, Sanwa Bank Ltd shed 50 yen to 1,350. Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd fell 90 yen to 1,960, dampened by news on Thursday that its U.S. unit had posted a loss from derivatives trading.

Brokerages were knocked lower by lingering concerns over possible ties with "sokaiya" corporate racketeers, brokers said. Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd fell 14 yen to 385. Daiwa Securities Co Ltd shed 20 yen to end at 887.
Nikko Securities Co Ltd fell 30 yen to 700. Scandal-tarnished Nomura Securities Co Ltd shares, however, ended flat at 1,370.

"The inherent strength of (Nomura) is preventing it from plunging," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said. "If the share price continues to be firm, investors may move to buy back the shares much sooner than anyone expects."
A handful of smaller issues backed by firm earnings all notched up gains. Advantest Corp added 70 yen to 6,250. Tokyo Electron Ltd rose 40 yen to 4,100.

Air transport, mining, railway/bus, pulp/paper and automobile were at the top of the list of gaining sectors. The decliners were led by banks, securities, land transport, miscellaneous manufacturers and electric power.

Brokers said there were hopes the government's plans to energise the stagnant real estate market, due to be announced on Monday, would provide stocks with support. But they added the plans will probably not send the market soaring.
"If they (plans) were earth-shattering, the government wouldn't wait until the last minute to announce them," a "Big Four" broker said.
"Bits of the plans would have leaked before the official announcement," he added.

In the coming week, market participants said there was likely to be some profit-taking, especially of financial sector issues, following the window-dressing period. But as the shares in the sector had weakened somewhat this week, there may not be a sharp plunge, they added.
-- Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-9052
